clinicalPearls: Pain localised to the coccyx (tailbone), classically exacerbated by sitting, especially on hard surfaces, and by rising from sitting
More common in women and frequently follows a fall onto the buttocks or childbirth, though some cases are idiopathic
Both obesity and, conversely, a very low body-mass index are recognised risk factors that alter how the coccyx is loaded when seated
Point tenderness is elicited directly over the coccyx, and a rectal examination can assess mobility and reproduce the pain
Dynamic sit-stand lateral radiographs can reveal abnormal coccygeal hypermobility or subluxation
Persistent or atypical coccydynia warrants imaging to exclude a rare presacral or coccygeal tumour such as a chordoma
Most cases settle with conservative care including a ring or wedge cushion, analgesia, and physiotherapy
Refractory cases may respond to image-guided local injection, and coccygectomy is a last resort in carefully selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Coccydynia is pain arising from the coccyx and its surrounding soft tissues. It often follows direct trauma such as a backward fall, or the strain of childbirth, which can produce coccygeal hypermobility, subluxation, or dislocation and inflammation of the sacrococcygeal joint and its ligamentous and muscular attachments. Abnormal sitting biomechanics, influenced by body habitus, concentrate load on the coccyx. In many patients no cause is identified (idiopathic), and rarely local pathology such as a tumour or infection underlies the pain.
additionalDifferentials: Pilonidal disease or other perianal and perirectal pathology
Presacral or coccygeal tumour such as chordoma or teratoma
Referred pain from the lumbosacral spine or sacroiliac joint
Levator ani syndrome or pelvic floor dysfunction
additionalInvestigations: Dynamic sit-stand lateral radiographs to assess coccygeal mobility and subluxation
MRI of the pelvis and sacrococcygeal region to exclude tumour or infection in persistent cases
Clinical rectal examination to assess mobility and reproduce pain
CT if bony detail is needed to characterise a fracture or destructive change
Diagnostic local anaesthetic injection to confirm the coccyx as the pain source
redFlags: Night pain, weight loss, or a palpable presacral mass suggesting a tumour such as chordoma
Fever or signs of local infection
reference.prognosis: The great majority of patients improve within weeks to months with conservative measures; a minority have persistent pain, but even these often respond to injection or, ultimately, coccygectomy.
pitfalls: Failing to exclude a presacral tumour in chronic, treatment-resistant coccydynia
Attributing pain to the coccyx when the source is the lumbosacral spine or pelvic floor
Proceeding to surgery without confirming the coccyx as the pain generator
references: Foye: Coccydynia review, Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation Clinics of North America
